source.title: BLUEFIN: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Financial Spreadsheets

answers.reasoning: Block 10 describes the judge's five-step perturbation procedure (read, change input, recalc, read, restore), and block 19 says an agent that never recalculates cannot check its own dynamic values. The page presents the recalc link as a correlation, so the causal story here is plausible rather than proven.
answers.answer: The judge changes an input, calls recalc_workbook, and checks whether the output moves to the correct new value. An agent that never recalculates never sees what its formulas actually produce, or how they respond to changes. Hardcoded intermediates, overwritten formulas or non-converging circular structures therefore go unnoticed and uncorrected, and they fail when the judge perturbs.

answers.reasoning: The page shows hardcoded values pass Output Validation but fail Perturbation (toy widget, Gemini's merger EBITDA link). Sign, date and rate errors would change the displayed numbers and so miss the ±2% tolerance.

Block 14 says modifying an existing workbook imposes brittle integration constraints from its formulas, layouts and references. The case studies in block 21 show integration failures such as off-by-one row links and hardcoded links.
answers.answer: Manipulation is harder because the agent must fit its work into an existing workbook's formulas, layouts and cross-tab references, which impose brittle integration constraints. Building from scratch is more flexible. In the OpEx case, Gemini linked to a blank cell and shifted every line by one row, scoring 32%, while GPT-5.5 mapped the rows correctly and scored 88%.
